query: W melts near 3422 °C, whereas Cu boils near 2562 °C, so conventional induction or arc-plasma casting cannot readily yield a uniform W–Cu material. Phase separation and void formation can impair thermal transport. Filling a W skeleton with molten Cu or Cu powder can leave defects; spark-plasma sintering and mechanical alloying can produce finer, more uniform structures but can also leave voids; vapor-coated W powders have been sintered to achieve near-perfect contact between the constituents; and metal 3D printing has also been explored. Starting from W particles or connected W regions within a Cu matrix for heat transfer under irradiation in fusion-reactor joints, what single intervention could overcome these limitations while preserving mechanical durability? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts an outcome relative to a named existing fabrication baseline, defines the processing and service boundaries, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment and observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Adding a small amount of nickel to the W–Cu precursor blend prior to sintering produces a transient Ni‐rich liquid phase at the W/Cu interfaces. This phase improves wetting and interfacial contact, thereby reducing void formation and phase separation, which in turn enhances thermal transport and maintains mechanical durability relative to current sintering methods.
generation.material_initial_state: A composite of tungsten particles or connected W regions embedded within a copper matrix that typically shows voids and phase separation issues when processed via conventional methods.
generation.intervention: Uniformly introduce a minor (approximately 1–3 wt%) amount of nickel into the W–Cu blend prior to sintering.
generation.conditions: The intervention is implemented during a spark plasma sintering (or comparable high-temperature sintering) process at temperatures above 950 °C (where Ni melts to form a liquid phase) but below the boiling point of copper, ensuring a transient liquid phase without degrading either constituent.
generation.structural_mediator: The transient liquid Ni‐rich phase that forms at the tungsten/copper interfaces, promoting enhanced capillary wetting, improved interparticle contact, and accelerated mass transfer.
generation.mechanism: During sintering, the melted Ni forms a wetting layer at the W/Cu boundaries, filling gaps and reducing residual porosity. Its presence facilitates interfacial diffusion and the possible formation of stable intermetallic phases throughout the cooling process, thereby bonding the two phases more effectively without compromising each individual phase’s integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared with composites made without Ni, the Ni-doped W–Cu composite is predicted to have lower void content, a more uniform interpenetrating microstructure, enhanced thermal conductivity, and mechanical properties that are at least as robust as the current methods (like SPS or vapor-coating).
generation.baseline: Current fabrication techniques (e.g., spark plasma sintering of W–Cu composites without an interfacial agent) which often suffer from phase separation and void formation, impairing thermal and mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold for sintering processes where temperature is controlled to enable transient Ni melting (around 950 °C to 1200 °C) and for service conditions relevant to high-heat, irradiation-exposed fusion-reactor joints; effects outside these processing or service windows are uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement magnitude in thermal conductivity and mechanical durability is uncertain and may depend on the precise Ni concentration and sintering parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of W–Cu composite samples using the same spark plasma sintering protocol: one group with a uniformly mixed 2 wt% Ni addition and one group without Ni. Characterize the microstructure (using SEM and EDS) to assess void density and interfacial continuity. Measure thermal conductivity and mechanical properties (tensile/compressive strength) for both groups.
measurements: Void density and interfacial morphology (via SEM and EDS)
Thermal conductivity (via standard thermal conductivity tests)
Mechanical strength (via tensile and/or compressive tests)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-doped samples do not show statistically significant reductions in void content and improvements in thermal transport and mechanical strength compared to the control samples, the hypothesis will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Diamond single crystal particles with Ti/Ni coatings were obtained by magnetron sputtering. The diamond gained more than 30% weight and the coating thickness was 10–20 μm. The interfacial diffusion and solid solution formation in coated diamond composites led to the increase of interfacial bonding strength. The interface bonding strength and mechanical properties of the composites without diamond coating decreased, due to the occurrence of graphitization at the interface and the formation of carbides. Compared with the composite with uncoated diamond, the density, hardness, transverse fracture strength and interfacial bonding properties of the composite with coated diamond were significantly improved. The wear resistance of the coated composites is obviously higher than that of the uncoated composites, because the coating on the diamond particles maintains a relatively complete crystal form in the SPS process and has a higher bonding strength with the HEA matrix. This improves the holding force of the matrix and gives full play to the excellent properties of the HEA.
